name: Kaonde / Kikaonde
catalog_citation: Wright, J.L. 2007. An Outline of Kikaonde Grammar. (Series editor Mubanga E. Kashoki.) Lusaka: Bookworld Publishers and UNZA Press. ISBN 978-9982-24-04-99.
catalog_locator: Ch. I Phonology, section 'Stress', printed p. 9 (PDF p. 10 of an unofficial online copy; scanned image, no text layer)
catalog_quote: Stress. In every Kaonde word at least one syllable is spoken with slightly more force than the others, though this is not so marked as in English. This syllable is said to be stressed. Sometimes a word may also have a secondary stress on another syllable. It is probably true that in the majority of words this stress falls on the next to last syllable, but there are so many exceptions to this that it cannot be stated as a rule. Stress can come on any syllable including the last in contrast with English. Kaonde stress is independent of tone. A stressed syllable may be high or low and a high syllable may be stressed or unstressed. Some random examples follow in which the stressed syllable is underlined and the high tones marked: muuntu 'person', kijiilo 'feast', kilújo 'right hand', kalómbwana 'little boy', mujilo 'fire', pémbela 'wait', lánguluka 'think', mulanguluko 'through', lukétekelo…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim on printed p. 9 of the held Wright 2007 scan; citation and ISBN match the imprint page. (2) Deciding source: a 55-page missionary grammar sketch (1977, reissued 2007 under Kashoki's editorship) with an impressionistic stress paragraph ('probably true that in the majority of words...'). Against Glottolog's 35-item bibliography, CrossRef, archive.org, HAL/theses.fr and the UNZA repository, nothing fuller exists: no reference grammar, no phonology monograph, no JIPA illustration, no instrumental study; so Wright is the best available and is held. (3) Why 'thin' rather than 'adequate': every other description read treats Kaonde as tone + length with no word stress - Kashoki 1978 (held, Language in Zambia pp. 70-71: syllables 'more or less evenly stressed', penult force possibly an artefact of lengthening, stress never distinctive

sources.quote: 'Kaonde language has two suprasegmental features, these are, tone and length.' Two level tones H/L (contour only on long syllables), lexical tone and length minimal pairs (maana/maana; malwa/maalwa). No mention of stress anywhere in the phonology chapter.
